sense: to a post or an office

terms.grammar: with two accusatives: aliquem cōnsulem facere; passive fierī
evidence: Nep. Them. 2.1: praetor ā populō factus
terms.comment: The plainest way to say who was given a post, whoever gave it. For the people electing, creāre (see election); for putting someone at the head of something, praeficere with the dative (see in charge).
To name someone for a post, as the augurs who put forward a new member (Lewis & Short); first of all simply to name, call by name.

evidence: Sall. C. 26.1: sī dēsignātus foret (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To mark out, and so to appoint to an office not yet entered: cōnsul dēsignātus, the consul-elect. It also means to point out, describe (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: appoint (a dictator, a consul): the formal word
terms.comment: Used of a magistrate naming a dictator or his master of horse; outside these phrases it means to say.

terms.gloss: appoint, set up (a guardian, an accuser)
terms.comment: To set up, establish: of persons, to put someone forward or appoint him to a role (Lewis & Short); also to decide, fix a day (see establish).

phrases.latin: ad quod gerendum praetor ā populō factus
phrases.english: appointed general by the people to fight it

phrases.latin: quō enim tempore mē augurem ā tōtō conlēgiō expetītum Cn. Pompejus et Q. Hortēnsius nōmināvērunt
phrases.english: for at the time when Pompey and Hortensius nominated me augur, sought by the whole college
